abstract: Mobility hubs are an emerging approach for encouraging more sustainable travel behaviours. However, many of the elements needed to ‘make’ a mobility hub already exist in communities. Railway stations, bus and tram stops, shared car parking spaces, docked and dockless bicycle or scooter parking, and many other facilities might already be present, and well known to users or surrounding communities. What may be lacking are the mapping and other software tools that might help practitioners, tactical urbanists or just anyone seeking to make transport systems more sustainable and easier to use from defining their own mobility hub and producing supporting informational material. This paper reports the development basic tools for creating maps and a poster, informational pillar or otherwise. Are there mobility offerings in your community? These tools, a printer and somewhere hang a poster might be all that is needed to spread the word.

# Introduction
Mobility hubs are an emerging approach involving shared electric cars, bikes and cargo-bikes, e-bikes and e-cargo bikes, or other vehicles. These might help in shifting towards more walking, cycling and transit-based travel through providing options or those, more occasional, trips that are otherwise difficult without a car. In some cases it may be that a range of offerings are already in place, especially where the private sector has already implemented car-, scooter-, bike- or other -share services. Converting such places into a ‘mobility hub’ may be within reach with just some minimal physical interventions such as signage and advertising. 

However, tools for transforming such locations into ‘mobility hubs’ do not yet appear to be readily available. Instead, individual agencies implementing mobility hubs appear to have been largely created signage, advertising and similar elements afresh and bespoke by on a site-by-site basis. Such creation might involve graphic design, mapping or similar and so limit the opportunities for trials, bottom-up implementation or other low-cost interventions by practitioners or (potentially through tactical urbanism and/or grassroots activism) sustainability-focused advocates or other actors.

This paper reports findings from case and design-based research seeking to
develop new tools to support low-cost mobility hub implementation. The rest of
this paper is structured as follows: the next section outlines the context for this
research, including brief discussion of mobility hubs and tactical urbanism. The
research methodology is then described, followed by presentation of the results,
which are then briefly discussed in conjunction with a conclusion identifying
directions for future research.

# Research context
The plethora of independent private-sector transport offerings now available, including car-share and dockless bike/scooter systems, may have helped towards development of the mobility hub concept. Although driven largely by start-up, technology and communications, and related sectors, various governmental agencies have sought to both: regulate such offerings; and make them more than the sum of their parts. Defining dockless parking locations, allocating dedicated carshare parking spaces, installation of branding and informational signage and similar efforts may help to provide geo-spatial context and collectivisation. As well, there have been some emerging problems, including with respect to inappropriate parking of dockless bikes/scooters (i.e. blocking footpaths), and risks and environmental impacts of recharging models that rely on batteries being collected and then charged elsewhere, often without the appropriate facilities to deal with electrical loads or battery fires [@Meigs:2023aa, @Zhang:2022aa] Shared electric mobility hubs, such as those currently being trialled in Ireland as part of the ROBUST project [@ROBUST:2025aa], may provide solutions to such problems by shifting the recharging of vehicles to be at a hub itself where appropriate parking, electrical connections and other equipment (importantly for fires involving lithium batteries) are outside and typically unenclosed.

Other challenges for implementers and communities, however, may relate to the difficulty of developing mobility hubs, including the planning processes and funding acquisition necessary to build new facilities. Mobility hubs might tend to be located in public road reserves, within parking facilities or otherwise where there may be less clear authority and power to make changes without widespread public, institutional and government approvals or buy-in. These may also often require outside expertise and/or involve top-down policy-making in which those making decisions might be somewhat removed from the real mobility needs of individual communities, or who may adopt ‘one size fits all’ approaches lacking responsiveness to local context. Research in public policy analysis has long been examining on such non-rational factors and how they might influence decision-making, but these tend to be overlooked in transport policy research [@Marsden:2017aa]. Instutionalism, political approaches, incrementalism and other public policy models, however, are clearly applicable to transport systems (see for example [@Reynolds:2017ah]). Important within these are the top-down, bottom-up and hybrid theories of implementation, which emphasise the influence that street-level bureaucrats can wield to obtain outcomes that respond to their local needs and context, including sometimes outcomes that might be in opposition to central policy directions (see @Weible:2009aa and others).

Perhaps of more relevance, however, is the field of tactical urbanism, which adopts many such bottom-up and grassroots approaches to defining and re-imaging public spaces, especially those spaces within road reserves and related to transport systems. Tactical urbanism can involve making changes to public environments, often unsanctioned, that sometimes question what urban space is for or the legitimacy of how it is allocated. “PARKing Day” provides an example, having started as lunchtime take-over of an on-street car parking space by an architecture firm, who rolled out some green grass and a park bench, paid the parking meter, and in doing so questioned the validity of using such spaces for storing vehicles instead of as a parklet for people. This has since grown into an annual event [@Lydon:2012aa; @Lydon:2015aa; @Davidson:2013aa; @Blumgart:2016ab; @Morhayim:2012aa; @Longhurst:2015aa].

Similar ‘pop-up’ or protest-based approaches have helped legitimise bicycle lanes, delegitimise car-use of bus lanes, and are sometimes used as more mainstream ways (amongst engineers and planners) to help build public and institutional support for implementation, including for the installation of transit lanes [@Fucoloro:2013aa; @News:2019ab; @TransitCenter:2018ab ;@Transportation-Studies:2019aa]. These build on or have similarities to various earlier approaches including street-reclaiming [@Dobson:2023ae; @Engwicht:1999aa; @Fotel:2009aa; @Institute:2015aa}, the invention of the first ‘woornef’ [@Guttenberg:1982aa; @Lydon:2015aa] and Local Area Traffic Management [@Damen:2017aa], as well as being evident in the make-up of current directions towards ‘Movement and Place’, ‘Complete Streets’ and Network Operation Planning approaches [@Delbosc:2018aa].

Despite the many names, variations and foci of these and other interventional and decision-making approaches, the call from @Marsden:2017aa to “pay greater attention to context, politics, power, resources and legitimacy” retains relevance. Participating in unsanctioned activities, especially for minorities or others who might attract higher levels of attention from authorities, can be a risk that might limit engagement in tactical urbanism or similar activities [@Douglas:2018aa]. Intersections between illegality, illegitimacy and the ill-enforced similarly exist in the context of street art and its place on a continuum that includes commissioned murals, counter-culturism and the avant-garde, graffiti and vandalism. @Killen:2021aa and @Killen:2017aa  explore these topics in the context of trains, but of relevance here, however, are questions relating to who is allowed to post a public notice, define a ‘mobility hub’ or otherwise share knowledge about transport options. Engineers, planners, operational managers, communications teams and others may have less need to engage in tactical-urbanist-type implementation given that they might already have legitimate authority to make changes to the built environment, at least within the scope of their employment and remit. However, pop-ups, trials, bottom-up and incremental approaches to implementation may still be of use, or even necessary, for such actors when seeking legitimacy for new, unusual or just controversial interventions. @Reynolds:2021ab define these as ‘pragmatic strategies for legitimation through implementation’ based on case research of such approaches helping in the implementation of Bus Rapid Transit in Curitiba and other forms of transit priority in Zurich, Melbourne and Toronto. Other strategies include building legitimacy before implementation using technical evaluation, vision-based planning and/or public decision-making processes; or avoiding impacts on those who might seek to delegitimise change. Basic signage, linemarking or the public display of travel information would appear likely to be relatively easy for many practitioners to implement within their own institutional setting. What may be lacking, however, are tools and standarised approaches to mobility hub information provision for quick and relatively easy adaptation to local contexts. Likewise, for activists, practitioners wishing to affect change outside the remit of their specific employment situation, or the general public there do not appear to be tools that might support tactical urbanism efforts related to mobility hubs. This might be particularly relevant for the ‘creation’ of a mobility hub out of already existing and geographically-proximate facilitates, which might not be immediately obvious to travellers but something informally well-known and readily apparent to those with local knowledge of the geography and community. Leaflets, posters for shop windows and community noticeboards, or even resources for a tactical urbanist to launch a ‘guerilla marketing’ campaign of posters, Do-It-Yourself (DIY) signage and websites, might be all that is needed to facilitate bottom-up action and empower communities to define their own hubs and advertise their pre-existing mobility services and related facilities.

What appears to be lacking in the research literature, or in practice, are the tools to quickly and easily produce the sorts of maps, analysis and interpretations that might support the definition of a place as a hub and the communication of its existing and potential mobility and other offerings. Mapping, signage and similar interventions in both the physical and virtual might usually tend to be produced on a bespoke (ie. Location-by-location) basis by specialist geographers and graphic designers, and involve commercially-controlled datasets or platforms. With the advent of crowd-sourcing, open data and the widespread availability of open source software, however, there is the possibility of developing location-bespoke, but generalised, mapping and similar tools useful for practitioners or others wishing to ‘mobility hub-erise’ some part of the urban environment. The methods used in this research to define what such tools might do, and then to deliver a software to more easily develop their own mobility hub mapping and informational materials, which might provide an initial version for future refinement, are therefore described in the following. 


# Methodology

\citet{Coxon:2018aa,Coxon:2021ab} outline 
various industrial design approaches and tools, 
as well as discussing their relevance and potential applicability 
to transport systems. 
Notable amongst these is the Double Diamond, 
which involves iteration across 
four phases alternating between: 
diverging (1) Discovery 
and then converging (2) Definition phases; 
followed by diverging (3) Development 
and convergence to (4) Delivery of a design output \citep{UK-Design-Council:0aa}. 

This study adopts this approach together
with case studies of existing mobility hubs. Case studies can be especially effective
when theory development is at an early stage and when there is a need to explore
phenomena within real-world contexts, as is the situation here. A challenge, however,
is the need to be seeking generalisable findings despite researching at depth within the
case contexts (@Yin:2018ab and others). Here the need to be seeking generalisable
findings is addressed directly by the form taken by outputs, namely: the research
produces a software of package tools for mobility hubs in any location, not just those
selected as cases
   
Hubs were visited in the UK^[Cases were selected from a larger sample available at https://www.como.org.uk/mobility-hubs/built-andplanned-hubs. *London*: South Woodford and High Street Wanstead; and in *Camden*: Charrington Street, Goldington Crescent, Werrington Street, Cranlegith Street, Brill Place, Doric Way and Chalton Street. *Bristol*: 1 Abbey Wood, UWE Frenchay, Horfield Library and Gainsborough Square. *Birmingham*: Huntingtree Park and Andrew Road] . Case selection for this study was somewhat constrained by logistics, but in line with the recommendations of the methodological literature, the cases selected included leading and particularly novel examples. Findings from site visits where synthesised through cross-case comparison to develop the design problem Definition. The Development was guided by standardised approaches to package development for the R language, chosen here because: it is open source and freely available, therefore supporting goals of developing an accessible suite of tools; it has an extensive set of packages for geospatial analysis and mapping; and there is a large community of users who might help support those with less experience in troubleshooting.

# Results
## Discovery

Information panels, maps and other guides to facilities and services were present at
some hubs, but notably not at those in London. This is likely because of existing maps
and other information at nearby tube stations, bus stops or otherwise, which may have
lessened the need for mobility-hub-specific signage and mapping. Figure 1 (left) shows
selected images of informational panels and signage found at the hubs in and Bristol,
which shared some common design elements such as including both local and area-
wide maps, iconographic representation of facilities, and directional information.
Notably, the Bristol hubs included green cubes mounted overhead hub facilities, which
appear likely to assist in finding hub elements in busy urban environments.
Mapping and informational material, however, often appeared to include some that
are not specifically ‘part’ of a hub (e.g. toilets within another facilities, shops, cafes).
This highlights a potential question for implementers: what services and facilities to
include as ‘part of the hub’, versus those that are just ‘nearby’? In the case of the
Transport for West Midlands hub at Andrew Road directional signage to, and
information about, bus services at the nearby Halesowen Bus Station (approx 50m
walking distance) is provided, but the hub has a different location-based name and
branding identity.
Some of the hubs included linemarked areas for shared e-bike, e-scooter or e-
cargobike parking, bicycle parking and secure parking lockers, although the offered
facilities and services varied by location. A lack of shade, weather protection and
drinking water was also evident at most of the visited hubs, even though many of the
parklet-type facilities included steel framing that might have accommodated open-
sided roofing or similar. A containerised “Library of Things” appears to have been
added later to one hub in Bristol, onto top of areas linemarked and sign-posted as for
electric scooter hire. This may provide an indication of the possibilities of using
modular components to expand, re-purpose or adjust mobility hubs as situations
change (consistent with @Stuart:2002aa), but also a need for signs and maps to be
easily adjustable to match, once the original graphic designers or implementers have
moved on^[See also @Reynolds:2017ah discussion of ‘The Garbage Can Model’].

The site visits perhaps also highlighted the importance of maintenance, activity^[c.f. @Jacobs:1961aa "eyes on the street"] and updates to match changing circumstances that might give a hub a sense of ‘place’. Hubs in Bristol perhaps provide an example with litter, non-mobility-related signage, space requisitioned for other purposes, and some sites advertising dockless shared vehicles but without these present in sufficient numbers (or at all at the time of visiting Gainsborough Square) all providing indications of potential post-implementation challenges related to mobility hubs.

# Definition

Findings from the sites visits suggest a wide variety of modes, services and facilities might be provided as part of the hub itself, as well as further services and facilities identified as being ‘nearby’ as an extension of the hub offer. This might suggest adopting an open-ended and expansionist approach to mobility hub definition. The consistency of branding at the Bristol hubs, especially with respect to the iconographic green cubes drawing attention to hub elements, might highlight the importance of proximity and line-of-sight in defining a mobility hub^[Although mapping at most hubs provided information about services and facilities within up to around 15 minutes walking distance, hub elements appeared to generally be located within relatively confined areas, generally spanning less than 50 metres. The Andrew Road hub provides an example towards the upper end, with the entirety of the hub and the nearby Halesown Bus Station encompassed within a radius of approximately 70 metres, and spanning slightly less than 200 metres if traversed by foot. In contrast, the South Woodford hub takes up approximately 15 metres of kerb space and is less than 100 metres from the nearest tube station, while some in Camden use space equivalent to only a few car parking spots.]

Definitions of the facilities, services and modes necessary to become a mobility hub appear likewise to be open-ended and inclusive, rather than some sort of minimum checklist that all sites must have^[CoMoUK’s pop-up mobility hub offering provide an example, with the basic option consisting of a 12 square metre parklet with
bike repair facilitates, and bike parking and/or bike share docking [@CoMoUK:0ab]]. @CoMoUK:0ab discuss six types of mobility hubs: “large interchanges/city hubs; transport corridor, smaller interchanges or linking hubs; business park or new housing development hubs; suburb/mini-hubs; small market town/village hubs; and tourism hubs” along with suggested components for each. Further types might include the ‘shared’ and ‘electric’ forms of mobility hub, as in the ROBUST sites, wherein the offered modes are available for hire and electrically powered respectively. Guidance from @CoMoUK:0ab also suggests: a timeline of 12 to 15 months to step through consultation, design, stakeholder engagement, tendering and construction, although this appears to relate to either unpowered mobility hubs or replaceable batteries; budgets are in the vicinity of 250k to 650k pounds; and that “mobility hubs work best when part of a wider sustainable transport network that provides active travel, public transport and shared transport options” [@CoMoUK:0ab].

The design problem here, therefore, appears be to allow creation of mobility hubs that: incorporate existing modes, facilities and services; minimise cost and timeframes, such that practitioners and tactical urbanists might build legitimacy through implementation (c.f. @Reynolds:2021ab) using minimal resources, incremental approaches that allow expansion one-hub-at-a-time, and that are scale-able; and allow for rapid iteration, revision or adjustment to account for changing circumstances.

# Development

Both the Brimingham and Bristol mobility hubs feature pedestal-mounted signage that
includes: the hub name; iconographic representations of hub facilities; directional
indications; and two maps. These maps are, respectively, of the local vicinity (a 5-10
minute walk) of the hub; and the surrounding area (a 15-20 minute walk). A starting
point for developing software packages to support creation of further mobility hubs,
therefore, would appear to be outputting similar maps of the local and surrounding
areas, composited together into an image of similar size to the pedestal signage
encountered during the site visits along with site naming and other information.
Figure 2 shows the output of software developed during this research.

Here the software has been used to create output for the Galway ROBUST e-mobility
hub^[Although as an example the ‘surrounding area map’ shown is for the Letterkenny ROBUST hub location so as to demonstrate the generalisability of the research outcomes.]. Key features of the developed software include the ability to highlight points of interest^[Various religious and medical buildings are highlighted in purple, while the library is shown in blue and nearby schools in orange.], as per the maps found in site visits, but might allow considerable flexibility for practitioners in choosing between colours, iconography or other symbols. A powerful aspect of adopting the OSM datasets is that settings can be adjusted by the user and new maps generated within
minutes. For example, the ‘surrounding area map’ shown in Figure 3 a slightly different OSM tile option is selected, and buildings recorded as “pubs” (rather than public buildings) are shown in blue. Another flexibility of this approach is that maps at other scales can be produced, including at small scales which might include individual hub elements (i.e. the e-bikes or car share vehicles) so that users can locate the various services and facilities.

```{r extract_osm_data_bristol, eval=FALSE, include=TRUE, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE }

crs_local_metres <- 27700
# Ireland 2157


### Create hub locations
hub_location <- lapply(hub_location, function(x) x %>% 
  st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), 
           crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(crs = crs_local_metres) %>% 
  st_cast("POINT"))


### Create hub locations
hub_location_metres <- lapply(hub_location, function(x) x %>% 
  st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), 
           crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(crs = crs_local_metres) %>% 
  st_cast("POINT"))

place_sf <- lapply(hub_location, function(x) x %>% 
                    st_buffer(dist = 2000) %>%
                    st_transform(crs = 4326) 
                  )


placebb <- lapply(hub_location, function(x) x %>% 
                    st_buffer(dist = 2000) %>%
                    st_transform(crs = 4326) %>%
                    st_bbox()
                  )
### based on https://github.com/ropensci/osmdata/blob/main/vignettes/query-split.Rmd

split_bbox <- function (bbox, grid = 2, eps = 0.05) {
    xmin <- bbox ["x", "min"]
    ymin <- bbox ["y", "min"]
    dx <- (bbox ["x", "max"] - bbox ["x", "min"]) / grid
    dy <- (bbox ["y", "max"] - bbox ["y", "min"]) / grid

    bboxl <- list ()

    for (i in 1:grid) {
        for (j in 1:grid) {
            b <- matrix (c (
                xmin + ((i - 1 - eps) * dx),
                ymin + ((j - 1 - eps) * dy),
                xmin + ((i + eps) * dx),
                ymin + ((j + eps) * dy)
            ),
            nrow = 2,
            dimnames = dimnames (bbox)
            )

            bboxl <- append (bboxl, list (b))
        }
    }
    bboxl
}

bb_vector <- place_sf[[1]] %>% st_bbox() %>% as.numeric()
bb <- data.frame(min = bb_vector[1:2], max = bb_vector[3:4])
rownames(bb) <- c("x", "y")               
                 
queue <- split_bbox (bb)
result <- list ()

while (length (queue) > 0) {

    print (queue [[1]])

    opres <- NULL
    opres <- try ({
        opq (bbox = queue [[1]], timeout = 25) |>
            add_osm_feature (key = "building") |>
            osmdata_sf ()
    })

    if (class (opres) [1] != "try-error") {
        result <- append (result, list (opres))
        queue <- queue [-1]
    } else {
        bboxnew <- split_bbox (queue [[1]])
        queue <- append (bboxnew, queue [-1])
    }
}
final_building <- do.call (c, result)
list.save(final_building, "data/bristol_buildings_260608.rdata")

### amenity

while (length (queue) > 0) {

        queue <- queue [-1]
    } else {
        bboxnew <- split_bbox (queue [[1]])
        queue <- append (bboxnew, queue [-1])
    }
}

final_amenity <- do.call (c, result_amenity)


list.save(final_amenity, "~/data/bristol_amenity_260608.rdata")
```

```{r mock_up_layout_with_maps, out.width = "80%", fig.align = "center", fig.cap = "Mockup of hub signage. Source: authors.", echo = FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, cache=FALSE, eval=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("graphics/dundrum_mock_up.png") 


addImg <- function(
  obj, # an image file imported as an array (e.g. png::readPNG, jpeg::readJPEG)
  x = NULL, # mid x coordinate for image
  y = NULL, # mid y coordinate for image
  width = NULL, # width of image (in x coordinate units)
  interpolate = TRUE # (passed to graphics::rasterImage) A logical vector (or scalar) indicating whether to apply linear interpolation to the image when drawing. 
){
  if(is.null(x) | is.null(y) | is.null(width)){stop("Must provide args 'x', 'y', and 'width'")}
  USR <- par()$usr # A vector of the form c(x1, x2, y1, y2) giving the extremes of the user coordinates of the plotting region
  PIN <- par()$pin # The current plot dimensions, (width, height), in inches
  DIM <- dim(obj) # number of x-y pixels for the image
  ARp <- DIM[1]/DIM[2] # pixel aspect ratio (y/x)
  WIDi <- width/(USR[2]-USR[1])*PIN[1] # convert width units to inches
  HEIi <- WIDi * ARp # height in inches
  HEIu <- HEIi/PIN[2]*(USR[4]-USR[3]) # height in units
  rasterImage(image = obj, 
    xleft = x-(width/2), xright = x+(width/2),
    ybottom = y-(HEIu/2), ytop = y+(HEIu/2), 
    interpolate = interpolate)
}
```

```{r create_area_map_small, eval=FALSE, include=FALSE, echo=FALSE, fig.fullwidth = TRUE, out.width= "100%"}
    text.colour = "black", stat = "sf_coordinates", size = 2) +
  
 
  ### Walking radius

  st_as_sf(coords = c("xlim", "ylim"), crs = crs_local_metres) %>%

  theme(
```

## Delivery

The software developed in conjunction with this research is available online at <TO BE INCLUDED AFTER PEER REVIEW. CODE INCLUDED IN SUBMISSION>


# Discussion and conclusions

This design-based research has developed basic software tools that might be used in
the context of mobility hubs. The general format and styling is largely based on
elements in place at various mobility hubs in Bristol, but as discussed above the
flexibility of R might allow users to adjust layouts, styling and other details as desired.
As well as being freely available, the OSM online platform allows this dataset to be
edited by anyone, including for the purposes of mobility hub implementation
Clearly, there are many avenues for further research, including: expansion to produce
websites, posters, banners, leaflets and other informational products; developing
more generic materials for other purposes such as maintenance schedules, inspection
logs, management resources and other items that might help a mobility hub ‘product
owner’ facilitate operations, continuance and growth. Further development of ‘best
practices’ in mobility hub informational provision might involve additional case studies,
especially of non-UK sites, as well as improvements to the base ‘hub signage mockup’
developed here. There may be a need to better understand what facilities and services
might best be included as ‘part’ of a hub, as opposed to those that are mapped as
being ‘nearby’. More immediately, user testing and further development of the
software, and of the software outputs, especially the maps, would seem an important
direction for further research efforts in the short term.
This paper’s title asked a question related to the applicability of tactical urbanist
approaches to the topic of mobility hubs. Underlying this may be larger questions
related to ‘what is a mobility hub’ and ‘who gets to define and advertise something as
being a mobility hub’. Perhaps every railway station, bus or tram stop, shared or micro-
mobility facilities or many other places are already mobility hubs, but just no one has
put up a sign or handed out a leaflet that designates this as being the case? With
access to this software and a printer, turning the existing mobility offerings in your
own community into a defined hub may be within easier reach.
